aiExplanation: This function tries to find the **largest number that appears in exactly one subarray of length `k`**. It first builds a `Map` called `freq` that counts how many times each number appears in `nums`. It then notes the `first` and `last` elements of the array and starts with a result of `-1`. Looping over every distinct number, it only considers candidates when `k === 1` (every element is its own subarray) or when the number is the first or last element (since those sit in only one window of size `k` when `1 < k < n`); among those, it keeps the largest number whose `count` is exactly `1`. The logic is incomplete because it doesn't handle the `k === n` case (a single window containing everything, where any number qualifies) and doesn't cope with the first and last elements being equal, which is why this attempt is marked as failed.

author: Vitor
notes: Seems crazy to me that someone created an exercise that needs 3 different solutions within itself.
aiExplanation: This function finds the **largest number that appears in exactly one subarray of length `k`** by splitting the problem into three cases. If `k === n`, there is only one subarray (the whole array), so every number qualifies and it simply returns `Math.max(...nums)`. Otherwise it builds a `freq` map counting how often each number occurs; when `k === 1`, every element is its own window, so a number appears in exactly one window only if it occurs once overall, and the function returns the largest such number (or `-1` via `Math.max(-1, ...)` if none exist). For any other `k`, only the `first` and `last` elements belong to a single window, and only if they occur just once in the whole array, so it checks their counts (`firstC`, `lastC`) and returns the larger qualifying one, the single qualifying one, or `-1` when neither qualifies.
